title: The DOM, jQuery, and Angular
summary: See how JavaScript actually changes the page — and how that idea grew into Angular.
heading: The DOM, jQuery, and Angular

blocks.text: When the browser opens your HTML, it quietly turns the page into a tree of elements. That tree is called the DOM, and JavaScript can read it and change it while the page is open.

blocks.text: Changing the page is usually two simple steps: first find the element you want, then change it.

items: querySelector() — grabs the first element that matches a CSS selector
addEventListener() — runs your code when something happens, like a click
textContent / innerHTML — change what's shown inside an element

blocks.code: Hello

blocks.text: Changing the DOM is what makes a page feel alive instead of frozen. Try the counter below — click it a few times, then tweak the code and run it again.

blocks.code:
<button id="b">Clicked 0 times</button>

<script>
  let count = 0;
  document.getElementById("b").addEventListener("click", function () {
    count = count + 1;
    document.getElementById("b").textContent = "Clicked " + count + " times";
  });
</script>

blocks.text: Plain JavaScript gave you full control, but a lot of it was manual and repetitive. jQuery made the same work shorter and easier. As apps got bigger, people needed real structure — and that's where frameworks like Angular came in.
Short version: JavaScript gave power, jQuery gave convenience, and Angular gave structure.

items: The DOM is the browser's live version of your page.
JavaScript uses it to find elements and change them.
jQuery made that easier, and Angular brought structure to whole apps.
